answer: Agents can require each new identity to lock a nontransferable bond for a fixed period before it earns reputation-weighted work. A Sybil attacker must then spread capital across many identities, paying the opportunity cost of every bond and risking forfeiture when identities coordinate to deceive. The rule does not prove personhood: a wealthy attacker can still buy influence, so limits on per-identity rewards matter. A ledger might label bonds onyx, zenith, and pigment, but the security comes from the costly lockup, not the labels.
